title: Sales is more than selling
caption: Three questions to work on together, not three proven causes of trust.

trust.question: Increase trust?
trust.qualifier: A possibility to earn, <ref>not an automatic result of outreach</ref>

conclusion: Learn before you depend on the cash

two-different-intention-results.description: Murphy et al.'s stated-preference meta-analysis found a median hypothetical-to-actual willingness-to-pay ratio of 1.35 across 83 observations from 28 studies, with substantial skew. Morwitz et al. found weaker intention–purchase correlation for new than existing products. Neither result gives a correction factor for a B2B prospect or proves that all purchase intentions exaggerate demand [1] [2].

murphy-hypothetical-bias.title: Murphy et al., A Meta-analysis of Hypothetical Bias in Stated Preference Valuation

morwitz-purchase-intentions.title: Morwitz, Steckel and Gupta, When do purchase intentions predict sales?

history-has-counter-evidence.description: Poppo, Zhou and Ryu report that continuity expectations mediate the positive history–trust relationship; with weak continuity expectations, longer history was associated with lower trust. Doney and Cannon found no effect of trust on current supplier selection after controlling for previous experience and performance, although trust related to anticipated future interaction. These abstract-level findings are not proof that early startup outreach causes trust or purchases [1] [2].

poppo-origins-of-trust.title: Poppo, Zhou and Ryu, Alternative Origins to Interorganizational Trust: An Interdependence Perspective on the Shadow of the Past and the Shadow of the Future

doney-cannon-buyer-seller-trust.title: Doney and Cannon, An Examination of the Nature of Trust in Buyer-Seller Relationships

commitment-is-not-trust.description: Anderson and Weitz studied idiosyncratic investments and commitment in 378 manufacturer–distributor pairs. That is evidence about commitment, not a measurement of trust; these concepts must not be interchanged [1].

anderson-weitz-pledges.title: Anderson and Weitz, The Use of Pledges to Build and Sustain Commitment in Distribution Channels

what-the-internal-learning-trial-tested.description: Both groups of 116 Italian startups received feedback training; the treatment group additionally learned predictive frameworks and rigorous hypothesis tests, performed better and pivoted more. The trial did not isolate sales contact, measure capacity limits or compare feedback with no feedback [1].

camuffo-scientific-approach.title: Camuffo et al., A Scientific Approach to Entrepreneurial Decision Making: Evidence from a Randomized Control Trial

test-an-offer-not-applause.title: Test an offer, not applause
test-an-offer-not-applause.script: Suppose our founder offers to help a workshop organise next week's jobs. She names the scheduling problem, proposes a price and asks for a conversation about a small trial. Now she has something concrete to discuss. Does the buyer ask about the trial? Ask about the price? Or decline the conversation? Write down the response.

learn-from-a-no.title: Learn from a no
learn-from-a-no.script: A workshop manager might say that scheduling is someone else's responsibility. Another might be interested, but not during its busy season. A third might not understand what would change. These imagined answers suggest different next questions. Ask who owns scheduling, when a discussion would make sense, or which part of the offer was unclear.

early-buyers-are-a-small-sample.title: Early buyers are a small sample
early-buyers-are-a-small-sample.script: Our founder starts with two people she already knows. Both enjoy talking about software. Before rebuilding the product around their suggestions, she should speak with other kinds of buyers too. Perhaps a team without a technical enthusiast. Perhaps a team with a different way of scheduling. Compare the responses before making a large commitment.

give-reasons-to-keep-talking.title: Give reasons to keep talking
give-reasons-to-keep-talking.script: I would give the founder a small promise she can keep. Send the agreed trial outline on Friday. Admit which features are not ready. Arrive prepared for the next conversation. These are practical choices, not a recipe that guarantees trust. The buyer still decides whether to continue. A first message does not settle that decision.

test-what-you-can-deliver.title: Test what you can deliver
test-what-you-can-deliver.script: Now imagine the buyer asks for a trial next week. Our founder has to check what that promise would require. Can the team import this workshop's existing schedule? Who will answer questions? Write down what is known and what still needs testing. This is a possible delivery problem to investigate, not proof that the team cannot deliver.

turn-contact-into-a-learning-loop.title: Turn contact into a learning loop
turn-contact-into-a-learning-loop.script: Start with an assumption: a workshop wants help with scheduling. Make a specific offer. Record the response. Choose the next test from that response. If the question was unclear, rewrite it and try again. Do not change everything after every call. The purpose is to make better decisions while pursuing customers who may actually pay.
